title: CEC, Buffering and Nutrient Retention in Root Media

content.overview: Cation exchange capacity describes a medium's ability to retain and exchange positively charged ions. It contributes to nutrient retention and buffering, but it does not tell a grower how much plant-available nutrition is present or whether the physical root zone is healthy.

vocabulary.definition: A positively charged ion such as potassium, calcium, magnesium or ammonium.
The quantity of exchange sites in a medium that can retain and exchange cations under defined conditions.
Resistance of a system to rapid chemical change, including pH change.

sections.title: Exchange sites act as temporary reservoirs
sections.body: Charged surfaces in organic matter and mineral components can retain nutrient cations and exchange them with the soil solution. Different media have different exchange behavior.

sections.title: CEC and buffering are related but not identical to fertility
sections.body: A high CEC can increase retention and resistance to change, but a medium still needs appropriate nutrients, water, air and pH. CEC alone cannot diagnose fertility.

sections.title: Media composition matters
sections.body: Peat, coir, composted materials and mineral components can differ in CEC and physical properties. Formulation should be interpreted as a system rather than from one laboratory number.

workedExamples: Two media with different CEC may respond differently to the same fertigation change even if initial EC is similar.
A high-CEC medium with poor aeration is not automatically a better root environment.
commonMistakes: Treating CEC as a direct fertilizer concentration measurement.
Ignoring pH dependence and media composition.
content.practicalApplication: Review media composition, CEC where available, pH, EC, water retention and aeration together. Use changes in crop and root-zone trends to evaluate whether the medium's buffering is helping or masking a problem.
content.summary: CEC helps explain nutrient retention and buffering, but root-zone performance depends on physical, chemical and biological properties together.
